skill_title: Distinguish strong vs weak acids/bases and apply Ka/Kb
notes: 20 items: 6 lifted, 14 fresh. Strong vs weak (degree of ionisation); Ka/Kb magnitude; pH/conductivity/concentration tests; common examples.

items.question: Distinguish between STRONG and WEAK acids in terms of ionisation in water.
items.expectedAnswer: A strong acid ionises completely; a weak acid ionises only partially (an equilibrium).
items.explanation: Strong: complete ionisation. Weak: partial ionisation (equilibrium). Different from concentrated/dilute (which is about amount).
options: Strong acids are concentrated; weak acids are dilute.
Strong acids ionise partially; weak acids ionise completely.
A strong acid ionises completely; a weak acid ionises only partially (an equilibrium).

items.question: Name THREE common STRONG acids and THREE common STRONG bases.
items.expectedAnswer: Strong acids: HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄. Strong bases: NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂.
items.explanation: Standard list of strong acids/bases that learners should memorise.
options: Strong acids: HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄. Strong bases: NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂.
Strong acids: CH₃COOH, H₂CO₃, HF. Strong bases: NH₃, CH₃NH₂, Al(OH)₃.
Strong acids: HCl, HF, CH₃COOH. Strong bases: NaOH, NH₃, KOH.

items.question: Four weak acids have Ka values: A = 4.5 × 10⁻⁶, B = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, C = 6.3 × 10⁻⁵, D = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴. Which is the WEAKEST acid?
options: A
B
C
D
items.explanation: Smaller Ka = less ionisation = weaker acid. Ka of A (4.5×10⁻⁶) is the smallest.

items.question: Two acids HX (pH = 2.7) and HY (pH = 0.7) have the SAME concentration. Which is the STRONGER acid?
items.expectedAnswer: HY — at the same concentration it has the lower pH, so it is more ionised.
items.explanation: Lower pH at the same concentration = stronger acid. HY ionises more completely.
options: HX — its higher pH means more ionisation.
HY — at the same concentration it has the lower pH, so it is more ionised.
Equal — the same concentration means the same strength.

items.question: For weak acid HX with Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, is [H₃O⁺] GREATER than, EQUAL to, or LESS than [HX] in solution?
items.expectedAnswer: [HX] >> [H₃O⁺] — the small Ka means the acid is only slightly ionised.
items.explanation: Small Ka ⇒ little ionisation ⇒ [HA] >> [H⁺]. The reverse would be the case for a strong acid.
options: [H₃O⁺] >> [HX] — the acid is mostly ionised.
[H₃O⁺] = [HX] — they are always equal.
[HX] >> [H₃O⁺] — the small Ka means the acid is only slightly ionised.

items.question: Two acid solutions at the same concentration light up two bulbs: bulb A (H₂SO₄) and bulb B (HNO₃). Which bulb is BRIGHTER and why?
items.expectedAnswer: H₂SO₄ — it is diprotic, releasing 2 H⁺ per molecule, so more ions conduct.
items.explanation: Both strong, but H₂SO₄ produces twice the H⁺ ⇒ more ions ⇒ better conductor.
options: H₂SO₄ — it is diprotic, releasing 2 H⁺ per molecule, so more ions conduct.
HNO₃ — it is a stronger acid than H₂SO₄.
Equal — both are strong acids.

items.question: Bulb B (HNO₃) and bulb C (CH₃COOH) — same concentration. Which is brighter? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: HNO₃ — a strong acid is fully ionised, giving more ions and better conductivity.
items.explanation: Strong = fully ionised = more ions. Weak = partial = fewer ions. Conductivity reflects ion concentration.
options: CH₃COOH — weak acids conduct better.
HNO₃ — a strong acid is fully ionised, giving more ions and better conductivity.
Equal — concentration alone sets the brightness.

items.question: A learner says: 'A 0.01 mol·dm⁻³ HCl solution is a WEAK acid.' Is this correct? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — HCl is a strong acid at any concentration; this solution is just dilute.
items.explanation: Common confusion. Strong/weak ≠ concentrated/dilute. HCl is strong at all concentrations.
options: Correct — low concentration makes HCl a weak acid.
Correct — HCl is weak below 0.1 mol·dm⁻³.
Incorrect — HCl is a strong acid at any concentration; this solution is just dilute.

items.question: 1 mol·dm⁻³ HNO₃ (strong acid) and 1 mol·dm⁻³ CH₃COOH (weak acid) light up bulbs A and B respectively. Which is brighter, and which solution has the lower pH?
items.expectedAnswer: HNO₃ is brighter and also has the lower pH (fully ionised ⇒ more H⁺).
items.explanation: Strong acid: brighter bulb (more ions) AND lower pH (more H⁺).
options: HNO₃ is brighter and also has the lower pH (fully ionised ⇒ more H⁺).
CH₃COOH is brighter and has the lower pH.
HNO₃ is brighter, but CH₃COOH has the lower pH.

items.question: Define Ka, the acid dissociation constant.
items.expectedAnswer: The equilibrium constant for acid dissociation: Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA].
items.explanation: Ka measures the extent of ionisation. Strong acids have Ka >> 1; weak acids have Ka << 1.
options: The equilibrium constant for acid dissociation: Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA].
Ka is the concentration of acid that ionises.

items.question: Order the following by ACID STRENGTH (strongest first): HF (Ka = 6.6 × 10⁻⁴), HCN (Ka = 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰), CH₃COOH (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), HClO (Ka = 3.0 × 10⁻⁸).
items.expectedAnswer: HF > CH₃COOH > HClO > HCN (larger Ka = stronger).
items.explanation: Larger Ka = more ionised = stronger.
options: HCN > HClO > CH₃COOH > HF.
CH₃COOH > HF > HCN > HClO.
HF > CH₃COOH > HClO > HCN (larger Ka = stronger).

items.question: Why does a weak acid show an equilibrium arrow (⇌) in its ionisation equation, while a strong acid shows a single arrow (→)?
items.expectedAnswer: A weak acid is only partially ionised (HA and ions coexist ⇌); a strong acid is fully ionised (→).
items.explanation: Single arrow = complete reaction (strong). Double arrow = equilibrium (weak).
options: A weak acid is only partially ionised (HA and ions coexist ⇌); a strong acid is fully ionised (→).
Weak acids are fully ionised; strong acids are partially ionised.
There is no real difference; both arrows mean the same.

items.question: Which of the following is a WEAK base?
options: NaOH
KOH
NH₃
Ca(OH)₂
items.explanation: NH₃ (ammonia) is a weak base: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ (only partial ionisation). The others are strong bases (fully ionised in water).

items.question: How does the pH of a 0.1 mol·dm⁻³ weak acid compare to a 0.1 mol·dm⁻³ strong acid of the same monoprotic kind?
items.expectedAnswer: The weak acid has a higher pH — it ionises only partially, giving fewer H⁺.
items.explanation: Same concentration, weak acid → less H⁺ → higher pH.
options: The weak acid has a lower pH.
The weak acid has a higher pH — it ionises only partially, giving fewer H⁺.
They have the same pH at equal concentration.

items.question: For acetic acid (CH₃COOH), Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Calculate the [H⁺] in a 0.10 mol·dm⁻³ solution.
Why is H₂SO₄ a strong acid only for its FIRST ionisation?
items.expectedAnswer: The first ionisation goes to completion (strong); the second (HSO₄⁻) is only partial (weak).
items.explanation: Diprotic acids often have very different Ka₁ and Ka₂. H₂SO₄: strong then weak.
options: Because both ionisations are equally strong.
Because the second ionisation is stronger than the first.
The first ionisation goes to completion (strong); the second (HSO₄⁻) is only partial (weak).

items.question: Define Kb, the base dissociation constant.
items.expectedAnswer: The equilibrium constant for base ionisation: Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B].
items.explanation: Kb is the base equivalent of Ka. Similar form: products/reactant.
options: The equilibrium constant for base ionisation: Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B].
Kb is the concentration of OH⁻ produced.

items.question: Why does ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) not fully ionise in water, while HCl does?
items.expectedAnswer: Its conjugate base (acetate) is a stable weak base that readily recaptures H⁺, so ionisation is partial.
items.explanation: Acid strength tied to conjugate base stability. Strong conjugate base = weak acid; very weak conjugate base = strong acid.
options: Because ethanoic acid is more concentrated than HCl.
Its conjugate base (acetate) is a stable weak base that readily recaptures H⁺, so ionisation is partial.
Because ethanoic acid has no ionisable hydrogen.

items.question: Which statements about H₂SO₄ are CORRECT? I. H₂SO₄ is a strong acid. II. H₂SO₄ ionises completely in both steps.
options: I only
I and II
II only
Neither
items.explanation: H₂SO₄ is a strong acid (statement I correct). But it only ionises COMPLETELY in the FIRST step; the second ionisation (HSO₄⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + SO₄²⁻) is partial.

items.question: Why is a concentrated weak acid NOT the same as a dilute strong acid?
items.expectedAnswer: A concentrated weak acid has much acid but only partial ionisation; a dilute strong acid has little acid but full ionisation.
items.explanation: Concentration (amount) and strength (extent of ionisation) are independent properties.
options: They are the same — both have the same [H⁺].
A concentrated weak acid is always more acidic than any strong acid.
A concentrated weak acid has much acid but only partial ionisation; a dilute strong acid has little acid but full ionisation.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_CONJUGATE_BASE_STABILITY: Doesn't link acid strength to conjugate base stability
